text: Fowl Cholera is caused by the bacterium Pasteurella, with both digestive and respiratory symptoms; it is an acute, highly contagious septicemic disease with high sickness and death rates, especially in ducks, though a chronic form is also common. Acute signs: sudden deaths may be the first sign noticed; wattles and combs turn blue before death; diarrhea starts watery and white, turning green and mucus-mixed. Chronic signs: abscessed wattles, swollen joints and foot pads, and cheesy material in the sinuses around the eyes. Necropsy findings: petechial (pinpoint) hemorrhages on the heart, spleen, intestine, and abdominal fat; enteritis and pneumonia; small yellowish necrotic spots on the liver; and in layers, fibrinous peritonitis with ruptured ova. Treatment: TMP+Sulfa and Tetracycline-family antibiotics are effective, but treatment should run more than 3 weeks since Pasteurella survives a long time in wet, shaded, organic-matter-rich environments.
